newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. ground troops on their way to Kuwait - minister.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ground troops on their way to Kuwait - minister.

text.p: Kuwait said on Monday more American soldiers were on their way to the Gulf Arab state to expand a U.S. military build-up to deter 1991 Gulf War foe Iraq.
"The (U.S.) ground troops, which are on their way to Kuwait will be in Kuwait soon, or sooner than later," Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah said.
"And if there are any other arrangements that need to be taken, in consultation with our allies, we will not hesitate to take them," Sheikh Saud told a news conference.
He did not disclose the nature of the arrangements but said: "There may be other deployments in the near future (in other regional states). We are not aware of them (now)."

Asked about deployment terms, he said: "We are not restrained by any time limit," suggesting that the force, expected to number less than 5,000, would stay in the tiny Gulf Arab state as long as Iraq posed a threat.

Sheikh Saud emphasised repeatedly that Kuwait had felt no hesitation in approving the deployment. "Our resolve to stand with our allies against this dictator (Iraqi President Saddam Hussein) is beyond any doubt."
"We would go to any extent to guarantee the security of Kuwait and to prevent the repetition of the 1990 catastrophe (Iraqi invasion of Kuwait)," he added.

The go-ahead ended a brief misunderstanding with Washington over a premature U.S. announcement of the deployment prior to Kuwaiti approval. The U.S. embassy said Kuwait had officially notified Washington of its decision to allow in the troops.
It did not disclose the size of the force. There are already 1,200 U.S. troops in Kuwait taking part in regular exercises.
"We are ready to face this threat together with our allies," he said. "There is a (Iraqi) military presence in the south... that creates concern over the security and stability of Kuwait."
He reiterated that stability in the vital oil-rich region cannot be achieved as long as Saddam remained in power.
"Stability and security in the region and Kuwait generally cannot prevail until Saddam's regime is removed. He is playing games with us here."

"We are not willing to play the same game he (Saddam) is playing. We are serious about...this situation. We will not tolerate further any movement on his part with regard to the threatening of the situation in Kuwait," Sheikh Saud said.

The current crisis with Iraq started earlier this month when Washington punished Iraq for intervening on August 31 in Kurdish factional fighting in northern Iraq. The United States launched 44 cruise missiles at air defence targets south of Baghdad on September 3 and 4.
Diplomats said the additional ground troops from Fort Hood, Texas would be seen as a defensive force, in contrast to the deployment on Friday in Kuwait of eight U.S. Stealth bombers.
"It's one thing to send in ground troops -- a few thousand men are not going to be able to invade Iraq. It can easily be presented as a defensive measure," one envoy said.
"But it's quite another to send in strike aircraft that can fly all the way to Baghdad."

Diplomats said Saudi Arabia, Washington's largest Gulf ally and one of four states visited by U.S. Secretary of Defence William Perry this weekend, was unlikely to lift its objections to attacks on Iraq.
"If the United States retaliates once more against Iraq without serious provocation I don't think it would be understood by the international community," a senior Western diplomat in Kuwait said.
Perry visited Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain and NATO ally Turkey before flying to London for consultations with his French and British counterparts.
